DOLFYN has been developed by Henk Krüs from Cyclone Fluid Dynamics BV and is available as open-source-software (www.dolfyn.net). It is a program for the analysis of complex flow phenomena:
• Turbulence models for high Reynold numbers

The program is a general unstructured 3D Finite Volume solver. Although it is possible to use volumes of any shape, for Post and Preprocessing it is more common to have only tetrahedra, Hexahedra or wedges with a triangular base area. This allows an easy connection to other Finite Element codes.

However, SOFiSTiK provides also higher polyhedra cell types of the so called "dual mesh". The solution is then obtained for the nodes of the primary mesh, which has strong advantages for computing time and precision in 3D.

DOLFYN has been adopted to the SOFiSTiK-environment by importing the mesh, material and boundary conditions from the data base and saving results for postprocessing into the data base. All Pre- and Postprocessing tools of SOFiSTiK may be used therefore.

The physics of a fluid flow follows rather simple conservation and material laws (mass, mo- mentum, energy). From the continuity equation for example we get the fact that in case of a reduction of the cross section, the velocity will increase. From the law of Bernoulli follows a loss of pressure, as the total energy is the sum of pressure, kinetic energy and geodetic height and a transient acceleration term:

Some physical effects as the compressibilty of the fluid may be neglected for practical appli- cations in civil engineering, however the general solution of the viscous flow and especially for turbulent wind is a rather complex task indeed.

The main reason for that is the fact that some effects happen on a very small scale. The large eddies of a meteorological situation with several 100 km dimensions are interacting with the smaller eddies down to very small structures.
A very important figure for the comparisson of flow within differnet scales is the so called Reynolds number:
u a mean velocity of the flow

For a groundwater flow with velocities of cm/sec and an effective diameter d from some mm we have Reynold numbers of approximately 10, while for a larger Building with a dimension of d=10 m, a wind velocity of 15 m/sec one has a Reynolds number of 10 Million!

Flow for small Reynolds numbers is called laminar, i.e. the stream lines are parallel and simple differential equations are sufficient to describe the so called potential problem. Starting from a certain Reynolds number a chaotic behaviour of the fluid particles will occur. The flow becomes turbulent and additional energy is exchanged.

For an incompressible flow two material constants, the density ρ and the viscosity ν or μ are sufficient. From conservation laws and equilibrium we have the basic Navier-Stokes-Equation:

To account for all possible effects within a numerical simulation (DNS = Direct Numerical Simulation) a very fine mesh is required, which would exceed the possibilities of even future super computers by far for practical Reynolds numbers above 10 000. A solution between those and those available within DOLFYN (RANS = Reynolds averaged Navier Stokes) would be a method where the large eddies are directly simulated, but the small eddies are dissipated numerically (LES Large Eddy Simulation).

For an acceptably effective solution of a wind flow problem we need simplifications which map the transient three dimensional case to the very last result of a static load case of wind pres- sures for the extreme case.
For a numerical analysis with a CFD-Program with high Reynolds numbers the wind velocity is separated into a constant mean value and a fluctuation along the time scale:

This yields more unknowns and more equations with more boundary conditions which have to be solved or closed somehow. For most cases the turbulence is accounted for by means of an additional viscosity. Then we have two parameters:
• The kinetic energy of the turbulences k [m2/sec2], calculated from the mean values of the turbulent fluctuations respective turbulence intensities:
• A length scale Lt, which is the Prandtl mixing length and might be taken as the dimension of the largest eddy or a structural width:

This value is correlated to the integral length scales, but there are 9 different values in the atmospheric boundary layer. Recommended values are the smallest dimensions of the body or the smallest (vertical) length scale. Near the ground, the distance to the ground multiplied with the Karman constant (0.4) is selected as upper limit in many cases.

The additional turbulent viscosity is defined with an empirical constant as:
In some cases it is sufficient to use a constant value, but more common are models with two additional equations for the turbulent energy and some dissipation rate.
• The best known is the k-ε model with the rate of dissipation ε [m2/sec3], describing the
energy conversion per time based on the Prandtl-Kolmogorov formula:

This model is rather robust, thus, the quasi standard in industrial applications. It is well suited for most 2D shear layers. Its weakness is relatively well known. It has problems with boundary layer separation (not very precise, often too short) and problems with curved stream lines, curved surfaces or sudden changes (rotating fluids) sometimes even with buoyancy. Excessive turbulence generation in stagnation points is a major concern. Thus enhanced models (e.g. RNG or RKE) have been developped, whioch are available in DOLFYN.
• There is also the so called k-ω Model with some kind of frequency ω [ 1/sec].
ω ≈ Cμ · Lt ; μt = ρ · k ω (2.9)

The model should perform better for retarded flow near the wall better than k-ε but has a Strong sensitivity for outer turbulence parameters. Thus a combination with k-ε as Shear-Stress Layer Model (SST) has been developped. Both modells are not available in DOLFYN.
Modells resolving the fluctuant values like LES are not available in DOLFYN so far.

Rather simple is the description of boundarys with an inlet or a smooth boundary of the analysis domain where the flow is parallel to that boundary. Here the components of the flow quantities are known and can be described easily. For the pressure we have similar to the rigid body problem in structural mechanics to describe a reference value in any point of the system. It is also common use to describe p = 0 for the complete outlet of a flow region. The pressures calculated from the program are depending on the viscosity, that is why they do not follow the classical Bernoulli-equation 2.1. Therefore, it is better to use pressure differences when obtaining loads from the flow pattern.

For the inflow boundary condition for the turbulent parameters there are numerous possibilities. Equations 2.6, 2.8 and 2.9 define recommended values for the inflow, however to avoid a dominance of the inflow conditions on the solution it is recommended to limit the turbulent viscosity. With the selection of a turbulent energy the values of ε or ω should then have at least some certain value, or if those parameters are selected otherwise, an increase of the laminar viscosity might be helpful.
The most simple form of a wall is the symmetry condition, which is the natural boundary con- dition describing a flow parallel to the wall without any interaction with the wall itself.

If the flow has friction, the fluid particles at a wall are fixed (sticky) and will have the velocity zero. Fluid particles in the vicinity will be decelerated by friction forces. For a Newtonian fluid we have a linear relation between stress and velocity gradient:

The region in the vicinity of the wall, where the velocity reaches 99 % of the asymptotic limit value in the infinity is called the boundary layer. Within a laminar boundary layer the energy transport is governed only by the above equation. The thickness of that layer is also depending on the length of the attached flow. With a certain length the layer will become turbulent, the shear stress will rise and we have a more convex shape of the velocity profile. For a

certain distance from the wall the flow is described by a logarithmic law. This is defined for the relative velocity y+ dependant on the height and either an absolute sand roughness height ks according to Nikuradse or an atmospheric roughness parameter zo:

For the lowest laminar part ( y+ < 5 ) we have u+= y+, then we have a transition zone and from ( y+= 70 ) we have the logarithmic law up to y+= 500.
If the value y+ is within that region, it may be checked only after an analysis, when the velocities are calulated.

For high precission requests the boundary layer itself should be modelled with a sufficient number of cells (approx. 10 over the height) on the other side the closest vertex must obey the rule ( y+ > 12.5 ). In [6] an optimal value of y+ ≈ 100 is recommended. However if the mesh size becomes very small it is recommendable to drop the wall boundary condition and to resolve the boundary layer with a mesh with y+ < 1.

The boundary conditions of natural wind are governed by the fact that all important effects take place within that critical lowest layer of the atmospheric boundary layer. SOFILOAD has fea- tures available to calculate those wind profiles according to the design codes and provide them as constant or transient boundary conditions for DOLFYN. DOLFYN has also the possibility to define a theroretical solution of the turbulent flow in the atmospheric boundary layer.
Within that subject a slightly modified form of the logarithmic law is used in general, yielding defined values also for small values of z:
Where z0 is the so called roughness height, which can be taken as the size of a characteristic vortex created by the friction. It is possible to define then an equilibrium state:
These equations are the base of the ABL boundary condition.

If the flow along an edge comes to region where the pressure rises, the velocity will become smaller. As the variation of the pressure is not so detailed as that of the velocity, we will have the effect, that only at the edge the velocity will become zero. The rest of the fluid will then detach from the surface and be deviated into the free field. After the point of detachement we

DOLFYN uses the Finite Volume Method with an own geometry format The geometric file (nodes, faces, volumes) with extension .dge is exported by SOFIMSHA. There are two principal variants:
• The primary mesh uses the existing elements as cells. The solution is calculated for the centre of these cells. This is the standard procedure for the finite volume method.

• The dual mesh is generated by a Voronoi-process based on the faces perpendicular on the element edges. The solution is then obtained for the nodes. The finite volumes are then polyhedra. This method has large benefits for the speed and precision for generated tetrahedra meshes in 3D.
For spatial systems the BRIC-elements are taken directly. Surfaces have to be described via QUADs or structural areas.

For planar systems SOFIMSHA will export for DOLFYN all QUAD-Elements as hexahedra with a thickenss of 1.0, the Volume-Patch number is generated from the properties of the QUAD. The edges of the QUAD become surfaces the patch numbers for those are taken from structural edges or boundary elements defined with SOFIMSHA.

DOLFYN boundary conditions are given for a total surface or a volume only, adressed by a unique region number. When exporting the mesh the user the primary group number will be used for this region number.

WALL sets the boundary condition for any wall or boundary region not belonging to IN or OUT.
• The simplest case would be SYMP, for this natural boundary condition the fluid will become parallel to the boundary without any other interaction of the fluid with the wall.

• SLIP / NOSL are simple boundary conditions for the fluid velocity (no adherence and fixed at a hydraulically smooth wall). Compared to SYMP a SLIP boundary will enforce the turbulence parameters k and ε to become zero.

• A definition of the roughness by an explicit value is the most elaborated definition of the behavior at the wall by a logarithmic wall law. This law is only applicable if the value y+ is larger than 1.0.

A transient analysis will be initiated by the specification of T. There are several possibilities to subdivide the analysis time.
First there are different possibilities for the time step itself:
Definition of N and T defines the size of the time step.
The size of the (n+1)th time step is established by multiplication of the nth time step with
TFAC. For larger numbers of time steps it is advisable to check the given values with a pocket calculator, as the time steps can grow rather high if TFAC and DTM are chosen improper.
On the other side one can define the total time of the analysis explicit or via the time steps.
• With an input of N ≥ 1, N is the number of time steps. The total time is the sum of all time steps.

• As an alternate definition T is considered to be the total analysis time if N is defined less than 1.0. N is then the factor for the first time step. (e.g. N 0.001 yields without a progres- sion a first time step of one/thousand of the total time T.)
Without definition of T a steady state analysis is performed, N will then be the maximum number of iteration loops.

DRAG creates the sum of forces types SPX,SPY,SPZ and the moments SPXX,SPYY,SPZZ. First the leading group of the defined sets of groups with DRAG commands are searched. Theo forces are then referenced to the point defined with the DRAG command and if a reference pressure is given converted to force coefficients which will be saved as well. With an appended ":F" or ":C" only the forces or only the forces or coefficients will be saved. Second the boundary region numbers are searched, the forces are then relative to the origin of the global coordinate system.

This command defines the most important parameters for the solution of the equation system. The properties of the different methods may be seen in the document DOL- FYN_VERIFICATION.PDF. Not all parameters may be selected for all variables, e.g. there is no differencing scheme for the pressure.

The default is LUX for UVW and KEPS as well as GAM for the temperature, which is suit- able for hexahedral meshes. Tetrahedral meshes are considerably worse than hexahedral or polyhedral. Thus schemes with a strong damping should be used.

On a first glance a Cylinder might be a simple problem, however it is rather a complex one. If one has a look on the measurements for the drag coefficient depending on the Reynolds number one can distinguish several regions, to be treated in the following text:
Figure 4.1: Wind coefficients for a cylinder
• A laminar region for Reynold numbers up to approximately 40, the selected case will have a number of 20.
• A region with a slower descent of the drag coefficient up to reynolds number of 1000, within that region we will have vortex shedding according to Karman.

• A region with a rather constant drag coefficient up to Reynolds numbers of approximately 300 000. This is called the subcritical region. As the suction at the rear is determining the drag coefficient, it has rather high values.

• A super critical region from Re = 300 000 to 3 000 000, where the laminar boundary layer becomes turbulent and is now able to follow longer the circular geometry, the drag coeffi- cient drops significantly .
• A transcrititical region from Re = 3 000 000 where the detachement point moves again to the front and the drag coefficient increases again.

For Reynolds numbers 20 and 100 there are extensive numerical examples available obtained with a Benchmarks of the DFG. (http://www.featflow.de/bench_all/node2.html) (directory dol- fyn.dat/cfd_cyl/dfg.dat) The fluid properties have been defined as: ρ = 1.0 kg/m3, ν = 10−3 m2/sec. The inflow condition is a parabolic distribution with a maximum value of Um, thus a
Figure 4.2: System for channel flow with cylinder
mean velocity of 2/3 Um. The Benchmark contains solutions with several Million unknowns on supercomputers.

The first test case is a steady 2D example with Um = 0.3 m/sec, yielding the Reynolds number Re=20. The following quantities should be computed: drag coefficient cD, lift coefficient cL, length of recirculation zone L and pressure difference ΔP.
The pictures of the flow agree quite well with the published reference.

This example (millau.dat) shows the evaluation of the stationary wind drag coefficients for a section of a bridge depending on the angle of attack. The section is taken from the Millau bridge in France (Width 27.75, Height 4.20 m), where results of a wind tunnel test are available for the construction stage and the final stage.

The first difficulty is given by the selection of the inflow conditions for the wind. For the original project extended CFD studies for the terrain have been performed, for the CFD and wind tunnel we have to generalize the inflow. The wind tunnel report gave a turbulence intensity of 9-10 %. Assuming a roughness of 0.30 m and a height of the bridge deck of 200 m, we get a turbulence intensity of 9.4 %. The integral length scale is 81.0 m.

For the service state wind shields have been added, which have been modelled in the wind tunnel with perforated plates with 50 % permeability. A perfect match of results should not be anticipated therefore.
An other question is if one should model the wind tunnel model (scale 1:75) or the real struc- ture. In that case we used the real world dimensions, which is recommended by us in general.
In that case a 2D-Analysis is performed. To select the analysis model properly one should take care of the parameters for some fundamental questions:

• Distance of the section to the boundaries above and below. If one selects to small dis- tances, the blocking effect will disturb the pressures obtained considerably. It is recom- mended to block at most 4 % of the flow area, better is 1 to 2 %.

Length of the area behind and the mesh density. If the mesh behind the section has a coarse mesh or is not long enough, vortices may not be modelled properly and the variation in time may not be obtained at all. Stationary mean values of the pressures may be obtained however in most cases with the k-ε-Turbulence model. The recommendation is to use an extension of 10 to 15 times the bridge width.

Length of area before and the mesh density In the incoming undisturbed flow a distance of 1.5 times the deck width is sometimes sufficient, but in this case the high viscosity of the inflow which will be disturbed by the bridge, creates an import zone of some extension before the bridge. The recommendation is to extend the mesh until a nearly constant inflow pressure is obtained. The mesh density is influencing the generated pressures. As the maximum pressure coefficient is 1.0 this is a good control measure of the mesh quality.

The mesh has been created with a mesh size of 0.12 m at the bridge and 2.0 m in the free filed, extending above and below by the deck width (6 % blocking), and in the direction of the inlet by a factor of 2.5 and for the outlet by a factor of 9.5 of the bridge chord.

For variant angles of attack the section is rotated within the model. Thus the program has to transform the resulting forces to the sectional coordinate system which is also the case for the results of the wind tunnel experiment.
